payload.name: nyquist-stability-criterion
payload.scope: To decide whether a feedback system is stable without solving the closed-loop characteristic equation: count how many times the open-loop response encircles the critical point and compare that count with the open-loop unstable poles, so designers can settle stability from the loop response alone.

definition.body: The nyquist-stability-criterion is a human-made stability decision rule for feedback systems: the closed-loop system is stable if and only if the number of clockwise encirclements N of the critical point -1+0j by the locus of the open-loop transfer function L(jw) equals minus the number P of right-half-plane poles of the open loop, i.e. when the closed-loop right-half-plane pole count Z = N + P is zero. Parameters: (1) the open-loop transfer function L(s) evaluated on the imaginary axis, w from -infinity to +infinity (the positive-frequency half suffices by symmetry); (2) the critical point -1+0j; (3) the encirclement count N, clockwise positive; (4) the open-loop right-half-plane pole count P; (5) the decision rule Z = N + P = 0. Unlike the Bode margin test it is an exact global test: it decides stability from encirclements, while gain- and phase-margins quantify the distance to the stability boundary. Unlike the sampling-theorem nyquist-criterion, it concerns the loop response of a feedback system, not the reconstruction of a sampled signal. Persistence mechanism: maintained as the core exact stability test in classical control textbooks (Ogata's Modern Control Engineering; Dorf and Smith's Modern Control Engineering), feedback amplifier and servo design practice, and control-engineering curricula, back to Nyquist's 1932 paper 'Stabilization of Regenerative Systems' (Transactions of the AIEE). e.g.: Ogata's worked example L(s)=K/[(s+1)(s+2)(s+3)]: stable below K=63, encircled beyond; Nyquist's 1932 application to regenerative amplifiers; the encirclement count read from a MATLAB nyquist plot of a DC-DC converter open loop | not: nyquist-criterion (the sampling theorem fs > 2*fmax, a different construct under the same family name); nyquist-plot (the drawing of the locus, not the decision rule); gain-margin (a scalar distance to instability, not the encirclement test) [formal: criterium stabilitatis | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

payload.name: loop-gain
payload.scope: To quantify the total signal amplification around one pass through a feedback loop, enabling designers to assess stability margins and shape frequency response.

definition.body: Loop-gain is a human-made analytical construct in control engineering that quantifies the total signal amplification around a single pass through a feedback loop, defined as the product of the forward-path transfer function G(s) and the feedback-path transfer function H(s). Parameters: (1) the forward-path transfer function G(s) describing the plant and controller; (2) the feedback-path transfer function H(s) describing the sensor and measurement path; (3) the loop gain L(s) = G(s)·H(s), a complex-valued function of frequency or Laplace variable s. Persistence mechanism: maintained as the central quantity in stability analysis (Nyquist criterion, Bode plots) and loop-shaping design practice, encoded in classical control textbooks (Ogata's Modern Control Engineering; Franklin, Powell, and Workman's Digital Control of Dynamic Systems), simulation tools (MATLAB's loopgain function), and feedback amplifier design methodology. e.g.: the loop gain L(s) = K/[(s+1)(s+2)(s+3)] of a unity-gain amplifier from Ogata's stability analysis; the loop gain of a DC-DC buck converter from Erickson's compensation design; the loop gain of an audio power amplifier measured at unity-gain crossover for phase-margin evaluation | not: forward-gain (the amplification G(s) alone, not the loop product); feedback-factor (the attenuation H(s) alone, not the product) [formal: amplificatio circuli | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

payload.name: gain-crossover-frequency
payload.scope: To name the single frequency at which a feedback loop's loop gain equals unity, the point at which the phase margin is read and the standard closed-loop bandwidth specification is anchored.

definition.body: Gain-crossover-frequency is a human-made stability-analysis construct in control engineering that names the frequency at which the magnitude of a feedback loop's open-loop transfer function L(s) equals unity (0 dB): w_gc such that |L(jw_gc)| = 1. Parameters: (1) the open-loop transfer function L(s) of the loop; (2) the unity-magnitude condition |L(jw_gc)| = 1, which fixes the frequency; (3) the phase of L read at w_gc, from which the phase margin phi_m = phi(w_gc) + 180 degrees is computed. It is distinct from the phase-crossover frequency (where phase equals -180 degrees, the gain-margin anchor) and from the 3-dB closed-loop bandwidth (where the closed-loop gain falls to 0.707 of its low-frequency value). Persistence mechanism: maintained as the standard reading point of Bode plots and the default loop-closure specification in control textbooks (Ogata's Modern Control Engineering; Dorf and Smith's Modern Control Engineering), amplifier compensation design practice, and loop-shaping methodology. e.g.: the gain-crossover frequency of a DC-DC buck converter control loop specified at 1/10 of the switching frequency; the unity-gain crossover of a compensated op-amp amplifier read from its Bode plot for phase-margin check; the gain-crossover frequency of a servo control loop used to set closed-loop bandwidth | not: phase-crossover-frequency (the -180-degree crossing that anchors gain margin, a different point on the same curves); bandwidth (the closed-loop 3-dB frequency, not the loop's unity-gain point); corner-frequency (a single pole's break frequency, not a loop property) [formal: frequentia crucis amplificatio | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]
